## Task T11 (narrative: work/T11/report.md)

### Arguments (5)

#### A-T11-001 — Physical time without a metaphysical shortcut (position: inference limit)

- Premises: Einstein’s relations preserve clock order., Rovelli’s histories and relational predictions survive removal of privileged external time.
- Bridge principles: A formal representation does not determine the full ontology of what it represents.
- Conclusion: These results do not establish a timeless conscious bearer.
- Claims: CL-T11-001, CL-T11-002, CL-T11-003, CL-T11-004, CL-T11-005, CL-T11-006, CL-T11-018; sources: S-T11-001, S-T11-002
- Strongest objection: An all-history representation may naturally motivate eternalist ontology.; strongest reply: Even eternalism contains earlier/later relations and does not identify a single experiencing mind.
- Unresolved issues: Interpretative merits of eternalism and rival ontologies remain open. No broad quantum-gravity or empirical-relativity review.
- Review: R11 (accept)

#### A-T11-002 — A timeless conscious foundation with temporal manifestation (position: conditional positive model)

- Premises: Suppose a conscious ground can know ordered contents in one non-discursive act., Suppose a non-temporal grounding relation can explain why a concrete history obtains., Suppose individual perspectives are grounded without requiring additions to the ground.
- Bridge principles: Explanatory and intentional priority need not be temporal priority., A timeless intention can be directed toward a whole history and its ends.
- Conclusion: Under these substantive assumptions M2 avoids the simple accumulation contradiction and could unify temporal order with conscious grounding.
- Claims: CL-T11-007, CL-T11-008, CL-T11-011, CL-T11-012, CL-T11-014, CL-T11-016; sources: S-T11-003, S-T11-005
- Strongest objection: The model may redescribe history without explaining its concrete existence or subjective individuation; a fixed act may not count as agency.; strongest reply: It posits an actual subject and reasons-guided dependence, rather than merely an abstract record; the absence of deliberation does not by definition exclude intention.
- Unresolved issues: Prove the proposed grounding relation intelligible and explanatory. Supply comparative reason to prefer mind over impersonal structure. Value and goodness require separate premises.
- Review: R11 (accept)

#### A-T11-003 — The tensed-knowledge challenge (position: conditional objection and reply)

- Premises: Suppose objective presentness is irreducible., Suppose perfect knowledge must encompass which events are presently occurring., Suppose tracking these changing truths requires intrinsic cognitive succession.
- Bridge principles: The presence of irreducibly tensed reality, not mere temporal order, drives the inference.
- Conclusion: Then a cognitively perfect ground of this temporal world cannot meet H-T.
- Claims: CL-T11-009, CL-T11-010, CL-T11-015; sources: S-T11-004
- Strongest objection: A defender denies absolute presentness or argues one atemporal act knows every tensed fact through a non-successive access relation.; strongest reply: The first response rejects a key premise and is a serious alternative; the second must explain access without either missing changing actuality or collapsing all times into one temporal present.
- Unresolved issues: Neither A-theory nor B-theory settled here. Direct modern defender originals and response chain remain coverage gaps. Propositional and non-propositional knowledge need separate accounts.
- Review: R11 (accept)

#### A-T11-004 — Timeless personhood and intentional responsiveness (position: compatibility defense with temporal alternative)

- Premises: Necessary conditions of personhood must not be inferred solely from the way finite humans learn., A possible knower may have self-awareness and rational volition without deliberative updating., Responsiveness can be specified as dependence of effects on reasons, or as newly acquired awareness; these differ.
- Bridge principles: A capacity can remain unexercised; possible temporal exercise does not show the bearer already has succession.
- Conclusion: Simple personhood arguments do not automatically refute timelessness; actual interaction still needs a model.
- Claims: CL-T11-011, CL-T11-012, CL-T11-013, CL-T11-016; sources: S-T11-005
- Strongest objection: The proposed timeless capacities may be nominal; responsiveness to genuinely new events seems to require new states.; strongest reply: Either justify whole-history reasons-sensitive dependence, or accept a temporal divine life with creation. Neither option is cost-free.
- Unresolved issues: Craig’s timeless-without-creation scope is limited. Transition into time must not posit a time before time. Trinitarian illustration is an additional theological assumption, not universal-subject evidence.
- Review: R11 (accept)

#### A-T11-005 — Whole-history preservation versus survival (position: identity handoff)

- Premises: Representing or including all events of a finite life preserves specified contents., T01 H-S requires the same person’s subjectivity beyond irreversible bodily death.
- Bridge principles: A record or a containing knower is not automatically numerically identical to the represented person.
- Conclusion: M3 inclusion alone supplies a preservation proposal, not H-S.
- Claims: CL-T11-017, CL-T11-019, CL-T11-020; sources: —
- Strongest objection: An enlarged subject-history might include genuinely continuing subjectivity outside embodied succession.; strongest reply: That is a distinct stronger hypothesis deserving assessment under an explicit identity relation; merely calling it inclusion does not establish it.
- Unresolved issues: T13: bearer, death condition, numerical identity, continuation domain, memory and branching.
- Review: R11 (accept)

## Task T13 (narrative: work/T13/report.md)

### Arguments (5)

#### A-T13-001 — Psychological appropriation and a repaired continuity criterion (position: Positive conditional psychological account)

- Premises: A person is self-aware across relevant stages., Past experience can be appropriately appropriated despite changing matter.
- Bridge principles: Specify causal continuity without presupposing identity; add branching policy.
- Conclusion: Such continuity is a candidate basis for same-person persistence.
- Claims: CL-T13-001, CL-T13-002, CL-T13-007, CL-T13-008; sources: S-T13-001
- Strongest objection: Memories may duplicate, disappear or presuppose ownership.; strongest reply: Project repair: overlapping causal links and a nonbranching clause avoid direct-memory transitivity failure; they still need independent justification.
- Unresolved issues: Not all modern continuity accounts inspected; Parfit direct access failed. Locke’s own theory is not identical to this repaired project model.
- Review: R13 (accept)

#### A-T13-002 — Thinking animal and biological persistence (position: Positive conditional organism account)

- Premises: A human organism is present., It thinks., There is exactly one relevant thinker and that thinker is the person.
- Bridge principles: Identity preserves the organism’s genuine persistence conditions, once specified.
- Conclusion: The human person is that organism; a disembodied copy alone does not preserve it.
- Claims: CL-T13-003, CL-T13-004, CL-T13-009; sources: S-T13-002
- Strongest objection: A transplanted cerebrum seems to carry the person; or the strict thinker is a soul/constituted subject.; strongest reply: Olson presses costs of denying organism thought or multiplying thinkers; psychological evidence/concern may be mistaken for constitution.
- Unresolved issues: Unique-thinker and strict animal-thinking premises contested. Animalism alone is not a complete theory of death, resurrection or animal persistence.
- Review: R13 (accept)

#### A-T13-003 — Simple subject through qualitative change (position: Positive conditional irreducible-subject account)

- Premises: A hypothetical split leaves two equally psychologically supported candidates., There is a determinate fact about which, if either, is the earlier subject beyond the total qualitative facts.
- Bridge principles: Indeterminacy of accessible evidence reflects an additional bearer fact., That fact requires an immaterial essential part.
- Conclusion: A soul is the candidate identity bearer.
- Claims: CL-T13-005, CL-T13-006, CL-T13-007; sources: S-T13-003
- Strongest objection: Epistemic underdetermination does not entail an immaterial entity; deny further-fact premise or specify a physical/causal identity rule.; strongest reply: Charitable project reply: first-person numerical identity is not exhausted by descriptive similarity; the defender must argue that fact is real and immaterial, not merely unknowable.
- Unresolved issues: Short essay does not resolve all technical objections. A surviving soul and continuing experience require additional persistence/activation premises; simplicity is not immortality.
- Review: R13 (accept)

#### A-T13-004 — Enlarged first-person history beyond bodily life (position: Strongest project survival model)

- Premises: The foundation grounds a concrete first-person history, not merely an information record., The history includes subjectivity outside the embodied-life boundary., A defended relation unifies those portions as the same person.
- Bridge principles: Ordered content can be grounded without successive changes in the foundation., An explicit criterion—not resemblance alone—licenses same-subject attribution.
- Conclusion: M2 or enlargedM3 could satisfy H-S with foundation-level H-T.
- Claims: CL-T13-016, CL-T13-017, CL-T13-018; sources: S-T13-001, S-T13-002, S-T13-003
- Strongest objection: The asserted ownership/extension may restate survival; a universal knower can preserve a finite life without the person continuing.; strongest reply: Treat subjectivity and individuation as substantive ontology with identifiable constraints; this blocks dismissal by definition but adds explanatory/evidential costs.
- Unresolved issues: No observation here establishes enlarged history. Strict organism criterion rejects disembodied extension unless same-organism relation defended. Timeless individual model must explain non-successive awareness; the temporal-individual model does not solve that separate issue.
- Review: R13 (accept)

#### A-T13-005 — Temporal phenomenology under competing interpretations (position: Criterion-specific empirical comparison)

- Premises: Altered-time reports are documented as reports., Composite instruments mix distinct phenomenologies., Drug-context scale overlap is observed in one bounded design.
- Bridge principles: Phenomenological resemblance alone does not identify mechanism or ontology.
- Conclusion: The reports motivate investigation but do not discriminate H-T/H-S without timing, identity and access evidence.
- Claims: CL-T13-010, CL-T13-011, CL-T13-012, CL-T13-013, CL-T13-014, CL-T13-015, CL-T13-020; sources: S-T08-006, S-T13-004, S-T06-001, S-T07-007
- Strongest objection: Survival interpretation: coherent first-person reports and striking information may reveal real access beyond the body; instruments may miss their distinctiveness.; strongest reply: Ordinary alternative has demonstrated drug-context overlap, while the survival reply correctly notes that inducing a resemblance need not explain a given case. Seek prospective, independently scored information and resolved timing; separately ask what identity relation it supports.
- Unresolved issues: No same-mechanism conclusion; no inference of equal support. No result here crosses irreversible bodily death under H-S.
- Review: R13 (accept)

## Task P2T12 (narrative: work/P2T12/report.md)

### Arguments (4)

#### A-P2T12-001 — Eternal life with temporal effects and direct presence (position: Developed conditional timeless-ground model)

- Premises: An absolutely perfect being possesses its life completely without succession., Knowing/willing/awareness need not all inherit the temporal processes of human cognition., A relation across eternal and temporal modes can preserve their difference while permitting direct causal and cognitive presence.
- Bridge principles: Temporal location of an effect need not be temporal location of the agent’s act., ET′ direct-capacity clauses can be instantiated; the space/time analogy is relevant enough to challenge shared-mode objections.
- Conclusion: If those premises and bridges hold, an eternal agent can be cognitively/causally related to temporal persons without itself undergoing their succession.
- Claims: CL-P2T12-001, CL-P2T12-002, CL-P2T12-004, CL-P2T12-005, CL-P2T12-007, CL-P2T12-015, CL-P2T12-016, CL-P2T12-018, CL-P2T12-019, CL-P2T12-020, CL-P2T12-021; sources: S-P2T12-001, S-P2T12-004
- Strongest objection: Lewis1984P/causal actuality and1988existential-presence/tense arguments challenge whether the proposed relation can be actual or coherent, rather than merely named.; strongest reply: S&K1992argue against shared-mode requirements via nonspatial divine presence and make causal/awareness capacity explicit inET′.
- Unresolved issues: Joint satisfiability of the capacity clauses Objective tense versus cross-mode presentness Independent grounds for perfect being and immaterial mind Human constitution and persistence not supplied
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### A-P2T12-002 — The presentness objection and the exact later reply (position: Serious critic/reply assessment with version boundaries)

- Premises: Lewis1984allows calendar knowledge but treats present actuality as an objective additional feature., Lewis1988interprets classical existential presence as making all times ontologically equal., An omniscient timeless being cannot omit an objective feature of reality.
- Bridge principles: Direct presence across modes must be existential rather than merely representational., The critic’s objective-tense or ontological-parity account is correct.
- Conclusion: Under those premises the1981account either misses present actuality or commits to a tenseless ontology; the selected1992reply contests cross-mode premises but does not conclusively settle the tense dispute.
- Claims: CL-P2T12-007, CL-P2T12-008, CL-P2T12-009, CL-P2T12-010, CL-P2T12-011, CL-P2T12-012, CL-P2T12-013, CL-P2T12-014, CL-P2T12-017, CL-P2T12-018, CL-P2T12-019, CL-P2T12-020, CL-P2T12-021; sources: S-P2T12-001, S-P2T12-002, S-P2T12-003, S-P2T12-004
- Strongest objection: Defenders can challenge the necessity of shared mode and reject the critic’s assumed temporal-to-eternal transfer; temporalism is not established merely by insisting on it.; strongest reply: Lewis’s strongest1988case appeals to the metaphysical price of spatial analogies; S&Kacknowledge the absolute-present mismatch. Its additional moral argument is now separately examined as Lewis1986→Oaklander1987–88 in A-P2T12-004.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T12-001
- Unresolved issues: No1992directcitationto1984or1986 The separate1986moral argument has an inspected Oaklander reply; its premises and broader identity adequacy remain disputed Other named critics inspected only through1992attribution Later criticism not exhaustively searched
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### A-P2T12-003 — Eternal relation does not entail human survival or identity (position: Bounded project inference constraint)

- Premises: ET/ET′relate an eternal entity and a temporal entity without identifying them., An object being known or sustained does not specify its numerical identity across later episodes., A finite history may be represented or present to another subject without further human experience beyond that history.
- Bridge principles: Survival requires actual further subjectivity and a justified same-person relation, not only an eternal record or knower.
- Conclusion: The selected exchange cannot by itself establish enduring human consciousness, postmortem survival or a solution to branching/continuity; divine personhood and human identity remain distinct.
- Claims: CL-P2T12-003, CL-P2T12-006, CL-P2T12-022, CL-P2T12-023, CL-P2T12-024, CL-P2T12-025; sources: S-P2T12-001, S-P2T12-004
- Strongest objection: A broader dualist, resurrection or constitution theory might add a same-bearer relation and a reason to expect continued experience.; strongest reply: That would require its own defended premises and exact source evidence. P2T02was accepted only as a bounded derivative comparator and does not supply automatic survival.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T12-001
- Unresolved issues: Human individuation/constitution Continuation beyond bodilydeath Branching/psychological/organismiccriteria Empirical discriminating predictions The added Lewis/Oaklander exchange supplies identity analyses but no empirical identification or postmortem continuation evidence
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### A-P2T12-004 — Tenseless human persons, persistence and responsibility (position: Developed human-identity objection and actual direct reply)

- Premises: Lewis treats moral responsibility and temporally extended action as requiring a persisting agent., Lewis claims tenselessness permits only a temporal whole and its stages, and denies either can act or bear responsibility., Oaklander denies the asserted ontology is necessary and distinguishes whole-person identity, indexed properties and continuity analyses from stage identity.
- Bridge principles: Lewis’s conclusion requires his denial of a conscious, intending and responsible whole and his substantialist reading of persistence., Oaklander’s reply requires at least one defended account of persisting agency that does not import the disputed substantialist or tensed premises.
- Conclusion: The claimed necessary incompatibility of tenselessness with human moral agency is contested by explicit alternatives; the exchange supplies no general evidential identity criterion, postmortem continuation or timeless human mentality.
- Claims: CL-P2T12-027, CL-P2T12-028, CL-P2T12-029, CL-P2T12-030, CL-P2T12-031, CL-P2T12-032, CL-P2T12-033, CL-P2T12-034, CL-P2T12-035, CL-P2T12-036, CL-P2T12-037, CL-P2T12-038; sources: S-P2T12-005, S-P2T12-006
- Strongest objection: Lewis argues beyond stage nonidentity: a momentary stage cannot span an action, while a temporal whole allegedly has no consciousness, intentions or bodily members; a responsibility bearer must be more than a collection of events.; strongest reply: Oaklander distinguishes tenseless continuants without parts, the whole referenced through different stages, and psychological/physical continuity; the ordinary sameness condition does not alone entail a simple substance. His reply attacks the claimed necessity rather than settling every metaphysical account.
- Unresolved issues: Adequacy of indexed-property and token-reflexive analyses; Oaklander explicitly leaves tense debate open Whether the whole/continuity accounts adequately explain consciousness and agency Noncircular evidence, branching and interruption conditions not worked out No identified postmortem subject or actual timeless ground No actual later Lewis rebuttal established; Oaklander’s hypothetical rejoinder remains hypothetical
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-027 [philosophical_attribution]

Lewis1986 explicitly asks what human persons are and what it means for a person at one time to be the same at another; he excludes the separate question of evidence justifying a particular cross-time identification.

- Sources: S-P2T12-005 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Limitations: This supplies a developed metaphysical identity target, not an evidential test for identifying a surviving subject.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-028 [philosophical_attribution]

Lewis1986 argues that tenseless time requires persons to be extended composites with distinct temporal parts, and contrasts this with strict identity of an enduring person on a tensed ontology.

- Sources: S-P2T12-005 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Supporting claims: CL-P2T12-027
- Limitations: The asserted entailment from tenselessness to this ontology is disputed by Oaklander. Hoy, Chisholm and Swinburne are references within Lewis; their originals were not newly inspected.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-029 [philosophical_attribution]

Lewis1986 challenges assignment of responsibility both to a tenseless whole, which he denies is itself conscious, and to a present stage for an earlier stage’s deed; he also rejects bundles of stages as suitable responsibility bearers.

- Sources: S-P2T12-005 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Supporting claims: CL-P2T12-028
- Limitations: The whole’s alleged lack of consciousness and suitability for responsibility are premises of Lewis’s objection, not independently verified facts. This is stronger than merely noting that different stages are not identical.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-030 [philosophical_attribution]

Lewis1986 argues that embodied actions and many mental actions require an interval with a persisting agent; he denies that either momentary stages or the tenseless whole can perform such an action, concluding conditionally that tenseless persons cannot be morally responsible agents.

- Sources: S-P2T12-005 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Supporting claims: CL-P2T12-028, CL-P2T12-029
- Limitations: He allows the quoted Quinn discussion’s possible instantaneous mental acts or disembodied acts, while extending duration to many mental activities. The claim that a whole cannot have bodily members or intentions is contested; no empirical absence of agency established. His word perduring denotes persistence here; it is not adopted as a modern technical synonym for a temporal-parts ontology.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-031 [philosophical_attribution]

Oaklander’s journal reply explicitly identifies Lewis1986 and reconstructs its responsibility argument, then proposes three diagnoses: a false premise, an invalid inference between senses of persistence, or a question-begging substantialist assumption.

- Sources: S-P2T12-006 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Supporting claims: CL-P2T12-027, CL-P2T12-028, CL-P2T12-030
- Limitations: Actual direct reply relation established from body and reference, not title or publication order alone. This is not a Stump–Kretzmann1992 reply to Lewis1986.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-032 [philosophical_attribution]

Oaklander disputes that tenselessness entails temporal parts, citing Mellor and Butterfield and explaining a token-reflexive account of present-tense judgments with a strictly continuing person; he expressly declines to settle the tense debate and notes a problem with Mellor’s tenseless facts.

- Sources: S-P2T12-006 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth

- Limitations: Mellor/Butterfield are inspected only through Oaklander’s presentation; their originals and Oaklander’s separate1985 critique remain deferred. This reply to a claimed necessity is not an independently verified complete account of present experience.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-033 [philosophical_attribution]

Oaklander offers an account on which one person has temporally indexed properties without incompatible unqualified predicates, and separately distinguishes reference to a temporal stage from reference to the whole person whose stage it is.

- Sources: S-P2T12-006 ([object Object])
- Dependency group: Lewis1986–Oaklander1987–88 identity and responsibility exchange
- Reliability: original_attribution_supported; inference strength: source_assertion_not_premise_truth
- Supporting claims: CL-P2T12-028, CL-P2T12-031
- Limitations: These are proposed metaphysical analyses; numerical sameness of a whole is not derived from numerical sameness of its distinct stages. He uses enduring and continuant broadly enough here to include wholes with temporal parts; that usage must not erase the technical endurance/perdurance distinction.
- Review: P2R12 (accept)

#### CL-P2T12-034 [philosophical_attribution]

Oaklander sketches psychological continuity, including memory or other psychological connection, and physical continuity of a living human body as alternative analyses of persistence compatible with action and responsibility.

Oaklander distinguishes the ordinary requirement that responsibility involve the same persisting agent from the stronger claim that such agency requires a simple substance; his unsoundness, invalidity and question-begging diagnoses depend on keeping those readings separate.
